abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly embedded in software development work, reshaping how code is produced, reviewed, and maintained. Following the public release of ChatGPT and the expansion of the AI tooling ecosystem, developers now routinely encounter AI assistance in collaborative and security-sensitive contexts. Through interviews with eleven software developers familiar with generative AI tools and working across teams, we examine how developers adopt and evaluate AI in daily work, how AI use affects security-related practices, and how these tools shape collaboration and accountability. Our findings show that AI use is contingent and selective rather than habitual. Developers primarily rely on AI for low-complexity, low-accountability tasks, while deliberately limiting use in security-critical or system-defining work. Responsibility for correctness and safety is consistently framed as non-transferable leading many developers to refuse or limit AI use.

abstract: This paper introduces AlcoCircle, a framework for classifying alcoholrelated tracking applications across major digital platforms, including the Google Play Store, Apple App Store, and Chrome Web Store. Drawing from behaviour change theory, the framework organizes apps by purpose (e.g., alcohol reduction, abstinence support, consumption promotion), technical characteristics (platform compatibility, cost model), and ethical considerations (e.g., data security). By systematically mapping the alcohol app ecosystem, AlcoCircle reveals underdeveloped areas such as education and responsibleuse interventions and provides a foundation for evaluating and designing alcohol-related digital health tools. The framework is intended to support researchers, designers, and policymakers in advancing harm reduction, health promotion, and user-centred alcohol tracking technologies.

abstract: Health care reform debates have largely focused on cost and access, with less sustained attention to the underlying design assumptions that shape patient–provider relationships. We examine how dominant patient models influence engagement, responsibility, and care outcomes by adapting the Student-as-Client framework from education to health care. We reviewed patient role framings across academic literature and publicly available materials from health care provider networks, and examined these findings in relation to established models of student engagement in education. This analysis reveals how Patient-as-Product and Patient-as-Consumer models continue to dominate health care delivery, often limiting patient agency while externalizing responsibility for long-term health outcomes. We argue that a Patient-as-Client model offers a more appropriate conceptual foundation for interactive health systems, particularly in contexts characterized by chronic care needs, workforce shortages, and increasing reliance on digital health technologies. This paper positions patient models as design constructs that shape interaction, accountability, and trust.

abstract: Virtual reality (VR) characters are increasingly popular, yet they are often treated as singular personas despite being produced through the labor of multiple creators. While prior research has examined how virtual characters engage audiences, less attention has been paid to how creative labor is distributed and obscured between those who design virtual models and those who perform through them. To address this gap, we present a case study of Marcus the Worm, a VR character whose popularity highlights tensions between technical creators and on-screen performers. Drawing on community analysis, we examine how audiences attribute authorship and authenticity primarily to the actors who animate Marcus, while the modeler who constructed the character is pushed to the periphery. Our findings reveal “authorship collapse,” where multiple creative roles are flattened into a single visible identity. This dynamic shapes audience perceptions of creativity, ownership, and value, reinforcing unequal recognition within VR production ecosystems.
